↳ Posted by ceolachan on November 2nd, 2008.

The High Drive

I had an interesting conversation with Calum MacCrimmon recently about this tune. It was his opinion that the third and fourth parts were taken down from a live performance and that Duncan, being a master improviser, was simply flexing his musical muscles. I’m not sure one way or another, but I don’t believe he ever wrote down any but the first two parts. (After that conversation we played ‘The High Drive’ on stage - just the two part version!)

↳ Posted by Nigel Gatherer on July 29th, 2013.

The High Drive

On Circular Breath Gordon only recorded it as a two part tune but the music book produced later on has it in four parts. However, it is possible that the augmented version became so entrenched in sessions that it seemed churlish not to put it into the subsequent book of his tunes. I guess we’ll never know……… sadly. Two parts or four, it’s a cracking tune.

↳ Posted by Crieftan on July 29th, 2013.

The High Drive

I quite agree, Crieftain.

Speaking of the book - “Gordon Duncan’s Tunes” (2007), I think it’s a terrible shame and a disservice to Gordon’s memory that there are so many mistakes, stupid obvious ones at that. The proof readers should be ashamed, in my humble opinion.

↳ Posted by Nigel Gatherer on July 29th, 2013.

This is the Cape Breton influenced version of the tune played in some areas of the North Eastern United States.

Re: The High Drive

Regarding Gordon Duncan’s playing: on Just for Gordon, he plays all 4 parts, but not every time, in contrast to The Circular Breath, where he plays it as AABB. (2 A parts, 2 B parts, repeated several times).
On Just for Gordon, he plays it as AABB AABBCCDD AABB. Harmonically, the C and D parts are similar to the A and B parts, so he may just think of C as a variant of the A and D as a variant of the B.
